text: For fine harness only the firm part of the leather is used: the bellies and flanks are cut off, leaving a narrow strip called the back, from eighteen to twenty-two inches wide.
Most harness makers only moisten fine oak leather with a sponge and water and do not wet it to any considerable extent.

One leading manufacturer places all the straps in a vat of water until the grain shows signs of the tallow coming to the surface, then removes, wipes and hangs them until the surface moisture has dried off.
After vat-soaked straps are surface dry, the fitter rolls the whole lot in a coarse cloth and takes them out one at a time to fit them up.

Curriers condemn soaking fine, well-finished stock in a vat, but experience shows such leather works up into the finest harness with a soft, clear grain and smooth edges, and stays soft as long as leather that was only moistened.
Soaking the straps in a vat forces out a little oil and grease, but this can easily be replaced without harm, and the labor of fitting up is markedly reduced.
Well-tanned but poorly curried leather is far preferable to poorly tanned leather, however well curried, provided the harness maker treats it properly.
Well-tanned but poorly curried stock should be soaked until it is well moistened to the center; the time needed varies so much that the only guide is the appearance of grease on the surface.
A testing-strap is a small scrap of leather soaked in the water with the straps; the workman cuts it to see whether the moisture has penetrated to the center.
To clean badly fleshed leather, lay the strap on the bench grain side down, secure the end with an awl, and with a spokeshave cut off the loose scraps and thin, veiny portions.
No more of the flesh side should be cut away than is absolutely necessary, because cutting it away weakens the leather.
After cleaning, rub the flesh side with a slicker, lay the strap on a board grain side down, and brush on a coat of melted tallow, warm enough to run freely but not hot enough to injure the leather.
Straps coated with tallow should remain so for at least twelve hours, by which time the moisture has dried out and the tallow has struck well into the pores.
No bad results follow if leather stays coated with tallow much longer than twelve hours.

After the tallow has stood, place each strap grain side down and rub the flesh side thoroughly with a glass slicker, working in all the grease possible and removing the surplus. Then turn the strap over and rub the grain side to set the grain.
If the straps are to be worked up full, the grain side need not be rubbed much, because the rubbing during fitting up gives it a fine finish.
Recurrying improves the wearing qualities of leather as well as its looks: the rubbing makes the leather more dense and works the grease into every fibre, making it soft and flexible.
With ordinary leather, recurrying reduces the thickness by nearly one third without removing any of the original substance.
Recurrying benefits well-tanned but poorly curried leather more than it benefits poorly tanned leather, but in both cases the improvement repays the labor.
Leather for single-strap track harness should always be rubbed on the flesh side, so that after blacking the flesh side is nearly equal to the grain side.
The increased density that rubbing gives to leather makes it possible to trim the edges smoothly and finish them as finely as the grain.

Common harness leather is not recurried because the prices make it unprofitable; the straps are simply moistened by dipping them in a pail of water or with a sponge, using no more water than is necessary.
